hypotheses.builds_on: The concept is inspired by the paper’s focus on non-equilibrium evolution and general precedents in superalloy treatments that form protective oxides.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely introduces a controlled surface heat treatment as a method to influence the early evolution of the oxide scale, targeting improved corrosion and oxidation properties in non-equilibrium lightweight high-entropy alloys – a factor not investigated in the original work.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Minor doping with a rare-earth element (Gd) promotes grain boundary segregation that modifies the evolution of metastable intermetallic phases and enhances the stability of protective oxide scales during corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (e.g., an alloy similar to MgAlCuZn systems) produced by induction melting, exhibiting a complex microstructure with dispersed intermetallics and a predominantly solid solution matrix.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a minor addition of gadolinium (~1 atomic %) into the alloy composition, creating an MgAlCuZnGd variant.
hypotheses.conditions: Casting and processing parameters remain similar, ensuring the overall density remains below 6 g/cm³, with the only variable being the minor Gd addition.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Segregation of Gd atoms at grain boundaries and interfaces, leading to the formation of fine, stable Gd-rich oxide particles (e.g., Gd₂O₃) during subsequent oxidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Gd, as a rare-earth element, has a high oxygen affinity. Its segregation to grain boundaries promotes the nucleation of stable, adherent Gd-based oxides that act as anchor points for the formation of a continuous protective oxide scale. Simultaneously, Gd addition can alter the thermodynamics and kinetics of intermetallic phase evolution during non-equilibrium processing, potentially suppressing the growth of detrimental phases. This dual effect enhances resistance to both corrosion (by mitigating intergranular attack) and high-temperature oxidation (by stabilizing the protective scale).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The Gd-doped alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (lower oxide weight gain) and enhanced corrosion performance (lower pit density and current density) compared to the base alloy without Gd. The improvement is expected to be moderate in magnitude, though precise values require experimental determination.
hypotheses.baseline: The original Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without any rare-earth additions, showing a typical complex microstructure with standard intermetallic evolution and oxide formation.
hypotheses.boundary: Performance evaluations under identical conditions (e.g., corrosion in chloride-containing solutions and oxidation tests at temperatures around 600°C) with the only difference being the minor Gd addition.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The extent of improvement in corrosion and oxidation resistance may vary and is somewhat uncertain due to the complexity of Gd segregation behavior and its effects on phase stability.

paper_did: Developed lightweight complex concentrated alloy compositions in the Al‐Cu‐Si‐Zn‐Mg and Al‐Mn‐Zn‐Mg‐Si systems using semi‐empirical criteria, multi‐objective optimization, and CALPHAD modeling.
Synthesized the selected alloys by conventional induction melting in an inert atmosphere and cast them in copper molds.
Applied a heat treatment (400 °C for 20 hours with a slow cooling rate under protective atmosphere) to stabilize the microstructure.
Characterized the alloys through chemical analysis (ICP-OES), optical microscopy, SEM, XRD, and mechanical testing (compression strength and hardness).
paper_reported: The as‐cast alloys exhibited fine dendritic structures with a mix of predominant solid solution phases (e.g., FCC‐A1) along with several intermetallic compounds (e.g., Al2Cu, Zn2Mg in the Al‐Cu‐Si‐Zn‐Mg system and Al9Mn2Si, Mg2Si in the Al‐Mn‐Zn‐Mg‐Si system).
CALPHAD and non‐equilibrium solidification modeling predicted phase transitions and invariant reactions (e.g., transformation of BCC and Q‐phase components) as a function of temperature.

Heat treatment altered the microstructure (e.g., larger dendrite size and presence of micropores) while maintaining alloy composition within targeted ranges, and the mechanical properties were recorded in the range of 486–618 MPa (compression strength) and 268–283 HV (hardness).
paper_proposed: A strategy to further optimize alloy compositions using global multi‐objective optimization to better tune solid solution formation and intermetallic phase distributions.

Exploration of processing parameters aimed at achieving a more uniform dispersion of intermetallic phases, which could enhance the overall mechanical resilience and resistance in lightweight applications.

CALPHAD modeling and non-equilibrium (Scheil) simulations predicted temperature-dependent phase transformations and stability regions of both disordered (FCC, BCC) and ordered intermetallic phases.

Heat treatment led to coarser dendrites with well‐defined interdendritic phases and low porosity (less than 5 vol %), and the mechanical properties were found to be in the range of 486–618 MPa (compression strength) and 268–283 HV (hardness).

paper_did: Designed and produced a novel lightweight aluminum‐based complex concentrated alloy (Al58Mg18Zn12Cu5Si7) using industrial purity raw materials with an induction furnace and pour mold casting process.

Employed CALPHAD and thermo‐physical parameter calculations to predict phase formation and guide alloy design, targeting a multiphase microstructure with an Al‐rich FCC matrix reinforced by intermetallic compounds.

Conducted heat‐treatment experiments at 400 °C (24 h) and 200 °C (24 h) to study microstructural evolution, and characterized the as‐cast and heat‐treated states using optical microscopy, SEM/EDS, and XRD.

Measured key physical properties including Vickers hardness, compressive strength, and electrical conductivity, demonstrating that heat treatment decreases mechanical properties while increasing conductivity.
paper_reported: The alloy exhibits a predominantly Al‐rich FCC matrix interspersed with intermetallic phases such as Mg2Si and a ZnMgCuAl (C14 Laves) phase, with the phase fractions roughly matching CALPHAD predictions (≈20%).

Heat treatment resulted in a decrease in hardness (from 249 HV in the as‐cast state to 200 and 171 HV after heat treatment at 400 °C and 200 °C, respectively) and lower compressive strength (from 588 MPa in the as‐cast state to 495 MPa and 426 MPa), while electrical conductivity increased.
Observations of micro-segregation and dendritic structures were made, and the study confirmed that solid-solution hardening is the dominant strengthening mechanism in the as-cast alloy.
CALPHAD was found to overestimate the stability of certain phases (S-phase and Q-phase), indicating some variance between prediction and experimental microstructural evolution.
paper_proposed: The work suggests that further exploration of processing routes and property-tailored heat treatments could optimize the alloy for industrial applications in structural, automotive, and energy sectors.
Future studies are implied to assess application-specific properties, potentially adjusting microstructure and phase distribution to meet target performance criteria.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A short, intermediate-temperature anneal of the as-cast non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA promotes the precipitation of fine Mg-rich intermetallic compounds that act as nucleation sites for the formation of a contiguous, protective MgO-based passivation layer during high-temperature oxidation and in corrosive media.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) containing a mixture of metastable solid solutions and residual supersaturated matrix elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a short isothermal annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 350–450 °C for 1–2 hours) after casting to trigger controlled decomposition of the metastable matrix and promote fine intermetallic precipitation.
hypotheses.conditions: Annealing under inert atmosphere to avoid premature oxidation, followed by exposure to corrosive (3.5 wt.% NaCl) and high-temperature (oxidizing) test environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation and spatial distribution of fine Mg-rich intermetallic particles (e.g., analogous to the Laves phases seen in CuFeTiZrNix, but with Mg partitioning) that later catalyze the formation of a protective MgO layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: The anneal accelerates phase separation in the non-equilibrium alloy, depleting Mg locally in the matrix and concentrating it in nano-scale intermetallics. When subsequently exposed to high-temperature oxidation or corrosive environments, these localized regions preferentially oxidize, forming a dense MgO passivation scale that hinders further oxidation and corrosion. This mechanism builds on the concept that the formation of intermetallic compounds (as observed in nickel-containing HEAs [PMC9104004::web::008]) can influence protective oxide formation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared with the as-cast (non-annealed) baseline, the annealed alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion current density and reduced weight loss in immersion tests, as well as enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance, with at least a moderate reduction in corrosion rate.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast MgAlCuZnGd alloy in a non-equilibrium state, showing heterogeneous phase distribution and relatively less-developed protective oxide scale.
hypotheses.boundary: This hypothesis applies provided the alloy density remains below 6 g/cm³ and the annealing temperature and time are optimized to promote intermetallic precipitation without full equilibrium transformation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of intermetallic formation and the subsequent oxide scale evolution in the Mg-containing system are not fully established.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) induces extensive grain refinement and drives Mg segregation to grain boundaries in the non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA, leading to the formation of continuous, ultrathin Mg-rich oxide films during high-temperature exposure that significantly improve corrosion and oxidation resistance.

hypotheses.intervention: Subject the alloy to severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing) to reduce grain size to the nanometer scale and enhance solute (Mg) segregation.
hypotheses.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere to prevent premature oxidation, followed by exposure to standardized corrosive (3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) and oxidizing high-temperature conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A high density of grain boundaries enriched with Mg that act as rapid diffusion paths for Mg outward migration and provide sites for nucleating uniform, adherent MgO films.
hypotheses.mechanism: SPD increases the dislocation density and refines the grain size, thereby boosting the total grain boundary area. This increased boundary density drives Mg segregation to the boundaries due to its high diffusion rate. Under high-temperature oxidizing conditions, the Mg-rich grain boundaries preferentially oxidize, forming a continuous and well-adherent MgO layer that impedes further corrosive and oxidative attack. This concept is analogous to known improvements in corrosion resistance through grain boundary engineering in other alloy systems [TXT::wikipedia::Grain_boundary_sliding::013].
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally processed (coarse-grained) samples, SPD-processed samples are expected to show significantly lower corrosion current densities, enhanced passivation behavior in polarization tests, and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (thicker or more uniform protective oxide scales). The effect size is anticipated to be moderate to significant if grain refinement sufficiently enhances Mg segregation.

paper_did: Developed and processed a novel light‐density complex concentrated alloy with composition Al5Cu0.5Si0.2Zn1.5Mg0.2 by induction melting in an inert atmosphere and casting in a copper mould.
Applied a slow, controlled heat treatment (annealing at 400 °C for 30 h with slow heating and cooling) to modify the microstructure.

Carried out extensive microstructural characterizations using optical microscopy, SEM‐EDS, and XRD (and compared results with CALPHAD and kinetic simulations) to identify dendritic primary FCC phases and multiple interdendritic intermetallic compounds.
Measured mechanical properties via compression tests (yield strength of 500–600 MPa and ultimate strength of 800–900 MPa) and Vickers microhardness tests.

Evaluated corrosion resistance through potentiodynamic polarization, Tafel analysis, linear polarization resistance, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (with comparisons to A570 Gr 40 steel).
paper_reported: The as‐cast alloy exhibits a fine dendritic microstructure with multiple interdendritic phases, including intermetallic compounds such as Al2Cu, Mg8Cu2Al4Si7, and Mg2Zn11, while XRD analyses confirmed predominant FCC‐Al (and an A3‐Zn based phase).

Heat treatment changes the microstructure – refining phase morphology (e.g., formation of an Al4.2Cu3.2Zn0.7 phase) and leading to a more uniform distribution of phases – which correlates with a reduction in microhardness and modification of mechanical responses.
Mechanical tests indicate that the alloy has a competitive compressive strength (with yield strengths between 500–600 MPa), and the heat‐treated state exhibits altered plastic deformation behavior.

Corrosion tests show that the heat‐treated alloy provides significantly improved corrosion resistance (with a reduction in corrosion rate from 0.3424 mm/year in as‐cast samples to 0.1972 mm/year) compared to conventional steel.
CALPHAD and kinetic simulations predict phase solidification sequences and precipitation behavior that qualitatively agree with—but also differ in phase identification from—the experimental findings.
paper_proposed: Although no explicit future work is outlined, the paper implies that further optimization of processing parameters (especially heat treatment) and improved predictive modelling of phase evolution in such complex concentrated alloys are necessary for enhanced corrosion resistance and mechanical performance.

There is an implicit suggestion to better correlate simulation predictions with experimental phase identification and to explore processing–composition interactions for marine and transport applications.

hypotheses.mechanism: During rapid solidification, the sluggish diffusion of some species induces local compositional inhomogeneities. A carefully controlled low-temperature anneal prevents complete homogenization yet allows the stabilization of these fluctuations. When exposed to high temperatures, the Mg-rich regions preferentially oxidize to form a Mg-rich oxide layer. Concurrently, the surrounding Mg-lean regions oxidize to form oxides of other elements (such as Al or Cu), resulting in a dual-phase, interlocking oxide scale. This composite structure enhances the barrier properties, retarding further oxidation and reducing localized corrosion attacks. This approach builds indirectly on the principle observed in MC/MD evolution of SRCs in refractory HEAs (PMC7921137::web::010-012) but applies it to exploit non-equilibrium compositional heterogeneities.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to a homogenized alloy (via extended annealing), the preserved microstructure with compositional heterogeneity should yield an oxide scale featuring an inner Mg-rich protective layer interlocked with secondary oxide phases, leading to lower oxidation weight gain and improved corrosion resistance. The improvement is directional but the exact quantitative differences remain to be established.
hypotheses.baseline: The alloy processed solely by rapid solidification followed by extended annealing that homogenizes the composition.
hypotheses.boundary: If the low-temperature annealing is too short, the heterogeneities may not develop sufficiently; if too long, homogenization may occur, thereby eliminating the desired dual oxide formation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The spatial scale of stabilized compositional fluctuations and their exact role in oxide heterogeneity require further quantitative study.

paper_did: Performed hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations on the equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory high‐entropy alloy to mimic annealing at 1800 °C, starting from a random BCC solid‐solution and evolving the nanostructure via successive MC swaps.

Calculated thermodynamic properties (changes in enthalpy, configurational entropy, and Gibbs free energy) during the MC/MD evolution and demonstrated convergence toward equilibrium (after about 20–40 MC swaps).

Inserted and simulated edge dislocations in the evolved structures to estimate the critically resolved shear stress (CRSS) and thereby compute yield strength, with detailed analysis of dislocation core behavior, reaction mechanisms, and pinning by short‐range clustering (SRC).
paper_reported: A significant reduction in potential energy (ΔH reduced by ~75–80 meV/atom) and free energy (ΔG reduction of ~45 meV/atom) was observed upon annealing, indicating the role of configurational entropy changes driven by local chemical ordering.

The nanostructure evolution produced SRCs that converged in morphology after ~20 MC swaps and matched experimentally observed 10 nm domain sizes, while dislocation simulations showed that CRSS increased from ~435 MPa (random structure) to ~815 MPa (after SRC formation), leading to yield strengths that closely matched experimental values.

Detailed dislocation analysis revealed complex interactions including dislocation bowing, formation of dislocation loops, and dissociation reactions that are responsible for the extra strengthening observed in the annealed R‐HEA.
paper_proposed: The work suggests extending the computational approach to further study coupled thermodynamic and dislocation mechanisms, including the prediction of ductile-to-brittle transition behavior.

It points toward integrating physics‐based simulation frameworks within an ICME approach to better tailor processing routes (e.g., annealing treatments) for optimizing the structure–property relationships in high-entropy alloys.
